newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane rocket launches two satellites for Asia.
newsitem.headline: Ariane rocket launches two satellites for Asia.

text.p: Western Europe's 95th Ariane rocket blasted off from equatorial French Guiana late on Wednesday and placed into orbit two satellites for the booming Asia-Pacific market.

The Ariane 44LP rocket equipped with two solid and two liquid strap-on boosters lifted off at 8:08 p.m./7:08 p.m. EST into a cloudy night sky from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
Twenty minutes after takeoff space officials said the Thaicom 3 satellite separated from the rocket.
Thaicom 3 will provide voice, data and video services throughout Asia for the Bangkok-based Shinawatra Satellite Company. The 2.6 tonne satellite was built by France's Aerospatiale.
"Thaicom 3 will be the most powerful satellite that we will put into orbit," Henri Sala, Aerospatiale's satellite operations director told a pre-launch news conference.
Sala said the cost of Thaicom 3 -- satellite, launch, ground stations and insurance -- was over $200 million.
Four minutes later BSAT-1a, a 1.2 tonne satellite for the Tokyo-based Broadcast Satellite System (B-SAT), separated from the rocket.
B-SAT is a consortium of major Japanese broadcasters including NHK and the WOWOW group and provides direct broadcast services throughout Japan.

B-SAT declined to disclose the cost of BSAT-1a. Specialists estimated the cost of satellite, launch and insurance at over $150 million. The satellite was built by Los Angeles-based Hughes Space & Communications.
The Paris-based Arianespace company that launches the Ariane-4 rocket series has led the commercial rocket launch market for over a decade, capturing over half of the world's market.
Over a third of its business comes from the booming Asia-Pacific region where strong growth in telecommunications is expected to continue well into the next century.

"The market as seen from Arianespace is very good and we all have the impression that there is continued and stable market growth due to the high reliability of telecommunications systems by satellite ... This is a very important launch for the Asia-Pacific region," said Arianespace vice president Ralph Jaeger.
The company has successfully placed 128 heavy satellites into orbit since 1982 and said it now has firm orders to launch 39 satellites worth an estimated $3.4 billion.

It fears, however, its lead is threatened by American consolidation -- notably the merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta and the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp. by Boeing later this year.
The first more powerful, new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch last June in a major setback for the European space programme.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over operations of Ariane-5 early this year, but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is planned for September at earliest.
